title: Part I: Alternating Digit Sum Framework
content: The file defines alternatingDigitSum as a recursive function on List ℕ: the empty list maps to 0, a singleton [d] maps to ↑d, and a pair-headed list (d₀ :: d₁ :: rest) maps to ↑d₀ - ↑d₁ + alternatingDigitSum rest. The key lemma alternatingDigitSum_cons establishes the recursion a :: rest ↦ ↑a - alternatingDigitSum rest. The main theorem ofDigits_modEq_alternatingDigitSum proves that when b ≡ -1 (mod d), Nat.ofDigits b l ≡ alternatingDigitSum l (mod d) by induction on the digit list.
mathContext: When $b \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$, the powers $b^k \equiv (-1)^k \pmod{d}$ alternate in sign, so $n = \sum_k d_k b^k \equiv \sum_k (-1)^k d_k \pmod{d}$. For $b=10$, $d=11$: since $10 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}$, we get $n \equiv d_0 - d_1 + d_2 - \cdots \pmod{11}$. This is the classical alternating digit sum rule for divisibility by 11.

title: Part II: Divisibility by 11 as an iff Form
content: eleven_dvd_iff proves that 11 ∣ (n - altDigitSum 10 n) for all n : ℕ. This is stated as an integer divisibility (11 : ℤ) ∣ (↑n - altDigitSum 10 n), which is both cleaner (avoids subtraction underflow issues with natural numbers) and more general than the one-direction form. Three examples verify 11 ∣ 121, 11 ∣ 1001, and ¬(11 ∣ 123) by native_decide.
mathContext: The alternating digit sum of 121 is $1 - 2 + 1 = 0$, confirming $11 \mid 121$. For 1001: $1 - 0 + 0 - 1 = 0$. For 123: $1 - 2 + 3 = 2 \neq 0$, confirming $11 \nmid 123$. The statement $11 \mid (n - \mathrm{altDigitSum}_{10}(n))$ is equivalent to $n \equiv \mathrm{altDigitSum}_{10}(n) \pmod{11}$.

title: Part III: Truncation Rules for 7 and 13
content: Both seven_dvd_truncation and thirteen_dvd_truncation follow the same algebraic template: write n = 10q + r, construct the identity 10(q ± c·r) = n ± k·r where k is a multiple of the target divisor, then use IsCoprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left to cancel the factor of 10. For 7: c=2, k=21=3·7. For 13: c=4, k=39=3·13. The key equation is 10·(q ± c·r) = n ∓ k·r, proved by omega on the push_cast form.
mathContext: The 7-truncation rule: $7 \mid n \iff 7 \mid (\lfloor n/10 \rfloor - 2(n \bmod 10))$. Proof: $10(\lfloor n/10 \rfloor - 2r) = n - 21r$. If $7 \mid n$ then $7 \mid (n - 21r)$ so $7 \mid 10(\ldots)$; since $\gcd(7,10)=1$, we get $7 \mid (\lfloor n/10 \rfloor - 2r)$. The 13-rule: $10(q + 4r) = n + 39r$, using $\gcd(13,10)=1$.

title: Part IV: Digit Sum Rules via b ≡ 1 (mod d)
content: The private helper dvd_iff_dvd_digits_sum packages Nat.modEq_digits_sum into a clean iff form: when b ≡ 1 (mod d), n is divisible by d iff the sum of its base-b digits is. This immediately gives 14 theorems: three_dvd_iff and nine_dvd_iff (base 10), thirtyseven_dvd_iff and twentyseven_dvd_iff and nineninenine_dvd_iff (base 1000), ninetynine_dvd_iff (base 100), onehundredone_dvd_iff (base 10000), seven_dvd_octal, and base-4, -5, -6, -9, -14 rules for 3, 4, 5, 8, and 13.
mathContext: The unifying principle: $b \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$ implies $b^k \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$ for all $k$, so $n = \sum_k d_k b^k \equiv \sum_k d_k \pmod{d}$. Choosing $b = 10^j$ for appropriate $j$ turns this into a grouping rule: for 37, $10^3 = 1000 \equiv 1 \pmod{37}$ (since $999 = 27 \cdot 37$), so sum three-digit blocks. Similarly $10^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{99}$, $10^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{101}$.

title: Part V: General Last-k-Digit Framework
content: The theorem dvd_iff_dvd_mod proves the key abstraction: if d ∣ m, then d ∣ n ↔ d ∣ (n % m). The proof is elementary: obtain c with m = d·c, then n = (d·c)·(n/(d·c)) + n%(d·c), and d divides the first term, so divisibility of n reduces to divisibility of n%(d·c). This one theorem instantiates to: two_dvd_iff (m=10), five_dvd_iff (m=10), four_dvd_iff (m=100), twentyfive_dvd_iff (m=100), eight_dvd_iff (m=1000), sixteen_dvd_iff (m=10000), thirtytwo_dvd_iff (m=100000).
mathContext: If $d \mid m$, write $m = dc$. Then $n = m \cdot \lfloor n/m \rfloor + (n \bmod m)$ and $d \mid m \cdot \lfloor n/m \rfloor$, so $d \mid n \iff d \mid (n \bmod m)$. For $d=2$, $m=10$: $2 \mid n \iff 2 \mid (n \bmod 10)$, i.e., the last digit determines divisibility by 2. For $d=4$, $m=100$: the last two digits. This is the most general form, covering all powers of 2 and 5.

title: Part VI: Coprime Factorization Rules
content: The general coprime_mul_dvd_iff theorem proves d₁·d₂ ∣ n ↔ d₁ ∣ n ∧ d₂ ∣ n when Nat.Coprime d₁ d₂. This is Nat.Coprime.mul_dvd_of_dvd_of_dvd plus the reverse direction via dvd_trans. The instantiations six_dvd_iff (gcd(2,3)=1), twelve_dvd_iff (gcd(4,3)=1), fifteen_dvd_iff (gcd(3,5)=1) give the familiar combined rules. This is particularly useful for composite divisors whose prime factors are already covered by individual rules.
mathContext: For coprime $d_1, d_2$: $d_1 d_2 \mid n \iff d_1 \mid n \text{ and } d_2 \mid n$. This follows from the Chinese Remainder Theorem or equivalently from Bézout's identity. For $d_1 = 4, d_2 = 3$: $12 \mid n \iff 4 \mid n$ and $3 \mid n$, combining the last-two-digit rule with the digit sum rule.

title: Part VII: Casting Out Nines and Error Detection
content: casting_out_nines_add and casting_out_nines_mul are one-line proofs via Nat.add_mod and Nat.mul_mod. The error detection theorem casting_nines_error_detect is also one line: if a·b ≡ c (mod 9) fails, then a·b ≠ c, proved by contradiction. Part VIII provides examples showing that 123·456 ≡ 56088 (mod 9) and 12·13 ≠ 155.
mathContext: The ring homomorphism $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}$ preserves addition and multiplication, so checking $a + b$ or $a \times b$ modulo 9 requires only $a \bmod 9$ and $b \bmod 9$. The error detection rate is $8/9$: if a computation is wrong, the mod-9 check catches it with probability $8/9$ (the check is fooled only if the error happens to preserve the residue). This method was standard practice for arithmetic verification before calculators.
